header:
Stocks vs bonds,
explained with acorns

lines.text: Stocks lost 37%. Bonds gained 20%. Same year.
lines.say: Stocks lost thirty-seven percent. Bonds gained twenty percent. Same year.

lines.text: A stock is a tiny piece of a company. Squirrel owns part of the tree.
lines.say: Quick lesson. A stock is a tiny piece of a company. Squirrel owns part of the tree.

lines.text: A bond is a loan. Squirrel lends acorns and gets paid interest.
lines.say: A bond is a loan. Squirrel lends acorns, and gets paid interest to wait.

lines.text: That year was 2008: stocks -36.6%, 10-year Treasury bonds +20.1%.
lines.say: That year was two thousand eight. Stocks fell about thirty-seven percent, and ten-year Treasury bonds gained about twenty percent.

lines.text: Squirrel with 60 stock acorns and 40 bond acorns ended with about 86.
lines.say: A squirrel with sixty stock acorns and forty bond acorns ended the year with about eighty-six.

lines.text: But bonds are not a force field. In 2022, both fell about 18%.
lines.say: But bonds are not a force field. In twenty twenty-two, rates jumped, and both fell about eighteen percent.

lines.text: Stocks swing harder, but have tended to grow more. From 2018 to 2025, the S&P 500 had just 2 down years.
lines.say: Stocks swing harder, but over time they've tended to grow more. From twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-five, the S and P five hundred had just two down years.

lines.text: Stocks: growth and big swings. Bonds: steadier interest. Many portfolios hold some of each.
lines.say: Stocks have brought growth and big swings. Bonds bring steadier interest. Many portfolios hold some of each.

post.title: Stocks vs bonds, explained with acorns
post.ig:
Stocks lost 37%. Bonds gained 20%. Same year.
A stock is a piece of a company. A bond is a loan that pays interest.
In 2008, the S&P 500 returned -36.55% while 10-year Treasuries returned +20.10%. A 60/40 acorn pile kept about 86 of 100.
But in 2022, both fell about 18%.
Sources: NYU Stern (Damodaran), S&P Dow Jones Indices via Slickcharts, SEC Investor.gov.
News and education, not financial advice.
